summary: Ventana Lunar answers two questions for any lunar south pole landing site and any date: will a lander have Sun for power, and will it see Earth for communications? Where both are yes, there is a landing window. It shows the answer on a 3D globe, a polar map, a month calendar and a first-person 3D view of the real terrain, and names the Deep Space Network antenna (Goldstone, Canberra or Madrid) that would be listening. The Sun and Earth come from JPL Horizons and are checked against the real LOLA horizon, so a ridge that hides the Sun or the Earth counts. Mission planners, students and the public can see in seconds when and where a south pole landing works.
details: What it does - For 29 curated landing sites (IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e, Apollo, the Artemis III candidate regions) and any point you drop a pin on, it tells you hour by hour whether the site has Sun, sees Earth, or both: a landing window. The four states have fixed colours and an always-visible legend, so the answer reads in five seconds. - Countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset, the month's share of Sun, Earth and windows, and a calendar strip you can scrub or play. - DSN mode: which Deep Space Network complex (Goldstone, Canberra, Robledo de Chavela) has the Moon in view, minute by minute, with the next handoff, and whether the site's Earth is high enough (3°) for a link. - The real horizon: each site's skyline from NASA LOLA elevation data. A Sun or Earth hidden behind a ridge counts as hidden, and a Sun seen over a lower skyline counts as up. Sites NASA's illumination maps place in permanent shadow are flagged. - A first-person 3D view from 2 m above the ground: real LOLA relief out to 128 km in levels of detail, the Sun and Earth at their true size and direction, hard shadows, lunar photometry, scanned Apollo 17 rocks (NASA Astromaterials 3D), and you can walk up to 1.5 km by tapping the ground. - "Open in LROC QuickMap" centres the official QuickMap on the selected site. How it works - A TypeScript simulator computes the sky in closed form (sub-solar point, the Moon's position, libration, Earth parallax). Over Nov-Dec 2026 it matches JPL Horizons within 0.04° in Sun elevation and 0.03° in Earth elevation, so answers are instant. Horizons data then replaces it, through our server, which caches the queries. - The server (Node + Hono) computes terrain horizons from the LOLA GDR grids (PDS) for any point and serves levelled terrain tiles for the 3D view. - The web app is Astro + React + Three.js and runs on a laptop without a GPU and on phones. It is installable and works offline, in English, Spanish, French, German and Italian, and follows accessibility rules (reduced motion, contrast, screen readers). Benefits and goals Landing at the lunar south pole is limited by low Sun angles, long shadows and a low Earth. Ventana Lunar turns ephemerides and terrain into one clear answer per site and hour, so mission teams, students and the public can compare sites and find windows quickly. Next steps: more sites, rover traverse planning and comparisons between sites. Tools: TypeScript, Astro, React, Three.js, Node.js, Hono, Vitest, Playwright, Docker, Dokploy.
